reason: This passage from Genesis 25 is told from an omniscient third-person narrative perspective rather than from the viewpoint of working people or regular folk. While the text includes depictions of work (Esau as a hunter, Jacob cooking stew), the narrative focuses primarily on patriarchal genealogy (תּוֹלְדֹת), divine prophecy (God's communication to Rebekah), and matters of succession and covenant—concerns of high-status family heads, not ordinary workers. The narrator is an external authority reporting on the inner states and relationships of Isaac, Rebekah, Esau, and Jacob, who are patriarchs of significant social standing, not common laborers or regular people telling their own story.
